entries.title: AUDIT.CATALOG.UNREAD — the catalog could not be read, so nothing was judged
entries.summary: An audit that read nothing and a database with nothing wrong produce the same empty report. This is the difference.

entries.title: CAP.L0.AMBIGUOUS_READ_HOSTS — the connection offers several read hosts and nothing chose
entries.summary: Laravel picks a read host at random. An audit that accepted that would describe a different server on different runs.

entries.title: CAP.L0.ASSUMED_VERSION_SKEW — the pinned version and the real server disagree
entries.summary: A pin makes a lint run reproducible. When the server it is compared against is a different version, findings are true about a database nobody deploys to.

entries.title: CAP.L0.CONNECTION_POOLED — the session is multiplexed, so instance-wide facts cannot be trusted
entries.summary: A transaction pooler hands your session to a different backend between statements. Anything an audit concludes about "this instance" stops holding.

entries.title: CAP.L0.DOWN_FAILED — the down() leg raised an error
entries.summary: While --roundtrip replayed the migration in a throwaway database, its down() raised an error.

entries.title: CAP.L0.DOWN_NOT_INVERTIBLE — down() did not restore what up() changed
entries.summary: The roundtrip replayed up, then down, then up again inside a throwaway database, and the second up failed.

entries.title: CAP.L0.INSTANCE_AMBIGUOUS — more than one connection could be the one to audit
entries.summary: An audit describes one database. When the configuration leaves several candidates and nothing chose, the run stops rather than picking.

entries.title: CAP.L0.INSTANCE_DIVERGENCE — the server is not the one the configuration describes
entries.summary: The configuration says one thing and the server says another. SQLens cannot know which is right; it can refuse to let one be read as the other.

entries.title: CAP.L0.INSTANCE_SCOPE_UNANSWERABLE — this instance cannot answer what the rule asks
entries.summary: A rule scoped to the write path reads perfectly well on a replica. That is exactly the trap: the value it returns describes the replica.

entries.title: CAP.L0.INVALID_IGNORE_LIST — the ignore list names something that is not a rule
entries.summary: A pattern matching nothing looks exactly like a pattern whose findings are gone. That is the same output for months.

entries.title: CAP.L0.MIGRATE_ERROR — Error during the real shadow migrate
entries.summary: The migration failed while it was being run for real against the throwaway shadow database.

entries.title: CAP.L0.MISSING_TOOL — an amplifier was registered and did not answer
entries.summary: An optional external tool could not run, so the checks it brings did not happen. Reported rather than skipped, because a smaller run must never look like a clean one.

entries.title: CAP.L0.NOT_CAPTURABLE — No capturable SQL
entries.summary: The capture ran to completion but produced no SQL to lint.

entries.title: CAP.L0.NO_ACTIVE_RULES — nothing was checked, and that is not a clean result
entries.summary: A level and category combination that admits no rule produces the same empty report as a healthy database. This is the difference.

entries.title: CAP.L0.NO_BASELINE_TO_IGNORE — `--ignore-baseline` was passed and there is no baseline
entries.summary: A flag that silently does nothing teaches a reader that it did something. This says it did not.

entries.title: CAP.L0.ORPHANED_IGNORE — an ignore entry that no longer silences anything
entries.summary: A suppression list nobody prunes stops describing what a project accepts and becomes a list of things it once did.

entries.title: CAP.L0.PINNED_HOST_DIVERGED — the server that answered is not the one that was pinned
entries.summary: A pin that did not take effect makes every finding a statement about a database nobody asked for, and it looks exactly like a real report.

entries.title: CAP.L0.PINNED_HOST_UNVERIFIED — the pin could not be checked against the server
entries.summary: The pin may be right. Nobody can say so, and a report that quietly assumed it would be asserting something it never confirmed.

entries.title: CAP.L0.PRETEND_ERROR — Error during the pretend run
entries.summary: The migration threw while it was being captured under pretend, so its SQL could not be linted.

entries.title: CAP.L0.RULE_WITHHELD_BY_DEPRECATION — a rule was not applied because it was retired
entries.summary: A deprecation makes the report shorter and leaves everything in it true, which is exactly what a clean run looks like.

entries.title: CAP.L0.RULE_WITHHELD_BY_VERSION — a rule was not applied because of the server version
entries.summary: A rule set that shrinks against an older server produces a shorter report in which every finding is still true and nothing says a check was skipped.

entries.title: CAP.L0.SERVER_BELOW_FLOOR — the instance that answered is below the supported floor
entries.summary: The audit ran and reported, but its verdicts may not describe this server.

entries.title: CAP.L0.SERVER_UNREACHABLE — the connection could not be opened, so nothing was audited
entries.summary: An empty report because the run never reached a database is not an empty report because the database is in good order.

entries.title: CAP.L0.SETTINGS_UNREADABLE — the server would not report its own configuration
entries.summary: Every server-baseline rule then has nothing to judge, and a rule with no subject reports nothing — which is what a healthy server also produces.

entries.title: CAP.L0.TENANCY_NOT_DECLARED — this project looks multi-tenant and has not said so
entries.summary: An audit across N tenant databases is not one statement. A report about whichever tenant was default reads exactly like a report about the application.

entries.title: CAP.L0.TENANCY_REFERENCE_MISSING — tenancy is `explicit` and no reference tenant is named
entries.summary: The project answered the question and stopped halfway. The run needs to know which tenant the report is about.

entries.title: CAP.L0.UNDETERMINED_CAPTURE — Capture could not conclude
entries.summary: Without this finding such a migration would contribute nothing to the run and vanish from it — the silent green the tool forbids.

entries.title: CAP.L0.UNOFFERED_HOST — the named host is not one this connection configures
entries.summary: A host pin that the configuration does not offer is refused, never dialed. Auditing a server the project never configured is worse than not running.

entries.title: CAP.L0.UNSUPPORTED_ENGINE — the engine that answered is not the one the driver names
entries.summary: The audit stopped without checking anything, and that is the honest answer.

entries.title: CAP.PRESCAN.INDIRECT_CALL — Indirect call from a migration
entries.summary: This migration reaches its effect through your own code — (new Backfill)->run(), app(Importer::class)->handle() — the most common way around the side-effect catalog.

entries.title: CAP.PRESCAN.INTROSPECTION_GUARD — Schema introspection guard
entries.summary: This migration's DDL sits behind a schema-introspection guard — if (!

entries.title: CAP.PRESCAN.RESULT_DEPENDENT — Result-dependent migration
entries.summary: This migration's SQL depends on what a query answers.

entries.title: CAP.PRESCAN.SIDE_EFFECT — Side effect in a migration
entries.summary: This migration would reach outside the database if it ran — a notification, an HTTP request, a queued job, a mail, a cache write.

entries.title: DEBT.LEDGER_MISSING — the account was expected on this machine and is not there
entries.summary: The one place where a missing file must not be read as an empty account.

entries.title: DEBT.LEDGER_UNREADABLE — the account is present and this build cannot act on it
entries.summary: Its own finding, separate from a missing one: an absent file and a corrupt file send you to two different places.

entries.title: DEBT.OBJECT_NOT_FOUND — the recorded object is not in the catalog
entries.summary: Not 'settled'. A dropped table, a schema outside this run's scope and a missing privilege all look exactly like this.

entries.title: DEBT.RESOLVED — a recorded debt the catalog shows as settled
entries.summary: Somebody finished it. Reported here and removed in the repository, never from a deploy server.

entries.title: DEBT.STILL_OPEN — the account records this debt and the catalog still shows it
entries.summary: An open end nobody finished, with its age attached. This is what the debt account is for.

entries.title: DEBT.UNRECORDED — a debt the database carries and the account has never heard of
entries.summary: The oldest debt in a project is usually this one: a constraint that predates the tool, reported on every run with no age and no way to acknowledge it.

entries.title: DEPLOY.CONTEXT.GRANT.OWNERSHIP_MISSING — the migration role holds every grant and still cannot ALTER
entries.summary: PostgreSQL does not let anybody grant ALTER TABLE. It requires ownership, which is why a grant check that stops at privileges can be green and wrong.

entries.title: DEPLOY.CONTEXT.READ_ONLY_TARGET — The instance this deploy points at will not accept writes
entries.summary: What the check reads on PostgreSQL and on MySQL, why a standby and a deliberately read-only primary are named separately, and what to do with either.

entries.title: DEPLOY.CONTEXT.SESSION_DEFENSE_NOT_APPLIED — The timeouts this run set on its own session are not in force
entries.summary: What the check reads back from its own session, why a `SET` that returned no error can still stop applying, and which connection to point the preflight at.

entries.title: DEPLOY.CONTEXT.SETTING — The settings this migration is about to run under, read instead of assumed
entries.summary: The four settings each engine reads right before `migrate --force`, why an ordinary everyday value becomes a finding at that moment, and what each one asks you to decide.

entries.title: DEPLOY.CONTEXT.VERSION_SKEW — the version CI checked against is not the server this deploy meets
entries.summary: What the check compares, what each of its answers means for the deploy, and which decision each one asks you to make.

entries.title: DEPLOY.DRIFT.DIVERGENT — Both sides have it, and describe it differently
entries.summary: The class where the tool is most able to be wrong about itself. What the field-level diff names, why the canonical form is what makes the finding trustworthy, and what to do when the two sides genuinely disagree.

entries.title: DEPLOY.DRIFT.MISSING_IN_DATABASE — The migrations describe it and the database does not have it
entries.summary: A migration that failed, was skipped, or was rolled back and never re-applied. Why the loud version of this finding is the harmless one, and how to tell a failed migration from one that never ran.

entries.title: DEPLOY.DRIFT.UNCOMPARED — One object type could not be read, so it was never compared
entries.summary: The finding that keeps an empty drift report honest. Why "no drift found" and "nothing was looked at" must not share an exit code, which side could not be read, and how to accept it deliberately without muting real drift.

entries.title: DEPLOY.DRIFT.UNEXPECTED_IN_DATABASE — The database holds something no migration describes
entries.summary: The hotfix-straight-into-production case: every migration ran, the deploy was green, and the schema still carries an object no file accounts for. What the comparison sees, what it cannot see, and why the next rebuild is the deadline.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_ENFORCED — A CHECK constraint that is not one
entries.summary: ENFORCED = NO is in the catalog, in SHOW CREATE TABLE and in code review — and admits every row it claims to refuse.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED — A constraint was added NOT VALID and the VALIDATE never followed
entries.summary: What an unvalidated constraint costs, the one moment it stops being free, and the single statement that closes it.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.INVALID_INDEX — An index a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` never finished
entries.summary: The leftover helps no query, costs every write, and makes the re-run fail on a name conflict. What the deploy gate reads, and what it deliberately refuses to do about it.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.INVALID_INDEX_NAME_COLLISION — an invalid index is standing where this deploy wants to build one
entries.summary: The same wreckage as a plain invalid index, except the migration about to run will fail on the name.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.ORPHAN_TRANSITION_OBJECT — An object whose name says it was meant to be temporary
entries.summary: users_old, tmp_backfill_state, orders_20260721 — what an unfinished expand/contract migration leaves behind, reported as a question rather than a verdict.

entries.title: DEPLOY.LEGACY.OSC_ARTIFACT — What an online-schema-change tool left behind
entries.summary: gh-ost's ghost table, pt-osc's triggers, InnoDB's #sql- temporary — names a tool generates, and one of them is still costing you a write on every row.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.CONCURRENT_INDEX_BLOCKER — a concurrent index build is about to wait on unrelated work
entries.summary: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY waits for every older transaction, not only the ones touching its own table. The build does not fail — it sits there.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.DISK_HEADROOM — How much space the pending migration will need, against what the instance can see
entries.summary: What the check estimates before a deploy, why the honest answer on a managed database is undetermined with the number attached, and what to do with that number.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.INACTIVE_REPLICATION_SLOT — A replication slot with no consumer is holding WAL
entries.summary: Which slot has no consumer connected, how much WAL it is holding, what the server's own wal_status says about it, and why the decision to reconnect or drop belongs to a human.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.LOCK_BLOCKER — Something is already holding a table this migration is about to lock
entries.summary: What the deploy gate reads out of the live activity views in the minute before a migration, what the finding names about the blocking session, and the decision it deliberately leaves to you.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.METADATA_LOCK_BLOCKER — a session is sitting on a table this migration is about to change
entries.summary: What is holding a metadata lock on the tables the pending migration will alter, and why an empty reading is only a pass when nothing went unread.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.MISSING_PRIVILEGE — the role running the migrations may not do what they ask for
entries.summary: What each engine is asked about the migration role, why a privilege MySQL cannot find is undetermined rather than missing, and the grant that answers the finding.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.REPLICATION_LAG — How far behind the replicas are, one moment before a migration adds to their work
entries.summary: What the check reads on each engine, the two states it reports, the line it judges against, and what to decide when a replica is behind.

entries.title: DEPLOY.PREFLIGHT.STATISTICS_UNREAD — the escalation could not read the object a finding names
entries.summary: An undetermined that keeps a lint verdict honest: the run could not measure the object, so nothing was raised.

entries.title: DEPLOY.RUN.TIME_BUDGET_EXCEEDED — The post-deploy run took longer than you allow
entries.summary: The one finding that is about SQLens rather than about your database. Why a run that hangs off every deploy needs a budget it can visibly break, why it is reported rather than aborted, and why sqlens:drift deliberately has none.

entries.title: GEN.L1.DML_WITHOUT_WHERE — the predicate you meant to type
entries.summary: An UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE touches every row. The statement is valid, which is the whole problem.

entries.title: GEN.L1.DOWN_MORE_DESTRUCTIVE — A rollback that destroys more than the migration built
entries.summary: Laravel rolls back by calling down(), and infers nothing from up().

entries.title: GEN.L3.DML_ON_SCHEMA_CHANGED_TABLE — the backfill runs while the schema lock is still held
entries.summary: Change the schema in one migration and fill the data in the next. Together, the lock lasts for both.

entries.title: GEN.L4.DOWN_MISSING — A migration that cannot be rolled back
entries.summary: Laravel rolls back by calling down(), and nothing else.

entries.title: LINT.ANNOTATION_UNKNOWN_RULE — an annotation suppresses a rule that does not exist
entries.summary: An `#[SqlensIgnore]` naming a rule id nothing answers to suppresses nothing — while carrying a mandatory reason, so it reads as a decision somebody weighed.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.ACKNOWLEDGED_GONE — a debt somebody chose to carry has stopped being detected
entries.summary: Deliberately not the same as a stale entry: an acknowledgment carries a written argument, and that is the thing that would be lost.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.ACKNOWLEDGMENT_EXPIRED — the decision to carry this debt was due for review
entries.summary: review_at is what keeps an acknowledgment from becoming permanent. This is it doing its job.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.LEDGER_UNREADABLE — the account exists and this build cannot act on it
entries.summary: Undetermined, never an empty account: a file this build cannot read must not be reported as a project with no debts.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.NOT_RECORDABLE — a recording run was asked for from a view that cannot support one
entries.summary: --debt=record needs the full pending set. One migration cannot tell an open debt from a settled one.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.STALE_ENTRY — the ledger holds a debt this run no longer owes
entries.summary: The project settled a debt and the file has not caught up. Bookkeeping, not a defect.

entries.title: LINT.DEBT.UNRECORDED — this run owes a debt the ledger has never heard of
entries.summary: An open end the account does not know about. Reported, never recorded: writing is a decision somebody makes.

entries.title: LINT.INVALID_CONFIG_REFERENCE — Your baseline names a rule that does not exist
entries.summary: A baseline entry for an unknown rule suppresses nothing while looking like a decision that still holds.

entries.title: LINT.NO_ACTIVE_RULES — the scope admitted no rule, so nothing was checked
entries.summary: A run that checked nothing and a run that found nothing produce the same silence. This finding tells them apart.

entries.title: LINT.NO_MIGRATIONS_READ — the run judged no migration at all
entries.summary: `--path` lints the pending migrations, and nothing is pending on a database that has been migrated. This finding is what stops that from reading as a clean run.

entries.title: LINT.SERVER_BELOW_FLOOR — the version this run reasons from is below the supported floor
entries.summary: The findings were still produced, and they may be wrong in both directions.

entries.title: LINT.SKIPPED — the run ended without linting anything
entries.summary: Nothing was pending, nothing could be captured, or the path matched no migration. Each reason is named.

entries.title: LINT.SKIPPED.MISSING_TOOL — an optional external tool is not installed
entries.summary: The rules that needed it did not run. They are named, and the run says so rather than reporting silence.

entries.title: LINT.SUPPRESSION_DEPRECATED_RULE — a suppression names a rule on its way out
entries.summary: The entry still works. It points at a check that will stop checking, and this names the rule that replaced it.

entries.title: LINT.SUPPRESSION_TOOL_RULE_UNDESCRIBED — a suppression names a tool rule this build does not describe
entries.summary: You may name a rule your installed binary emits without waiting for a release here. It is accepted, and said, because a namespace this package cannot spell-check is where a typo is likeliest.

entries.title: LINT.VERSION_PIN_UNREADABLE — the pin could not be read, and nothing was assumed instead
entries.summary: A malformed assume_server_version is not silently ignored. Version-gated rules report undetermined rather than guessing a version.

entries.title: LINT.VERSION_SKEW — the pinned version and the server disagree
entries.summary: Version-gated rules were applied for the version you pinned, not the one that answered.

entries.title: MY.L1.DROP_COLUMN — Dropping a column on MySQL commits itself
entries.summary: DROP COLUMN deletes the column and its data, and on MySQL no transaction takes it back.

entries.title: MY.L1.DROP_TABLE — Dropping a table on MySQL commits itself
entries.summary: DROP TABLE is DDL on MySQL, so no transaction takes it back — it is final the instant it runs.

entries.title: MY.L1.TRUNCATE — TRUNCATE in a migration, where no transaction takes it back
entries.summary: TRUNCATE in a migration's up() empties the table with no confirmation and no predicate to limit it.

entries.title: MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_CHARSET — Character-set conversion that copies the table
entries.summary: ALTER TABLE … CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET … re-encodes every value in every string column.

entries.title: MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_TYPE — Column redefinition that rebuilds the table
entries.summary: $table->…->change() compiles to ALTER TABLE … MODIFY, and MySQL's MODIFY takes the column's whole definition rather than a delta.

entries.title: MY.L2.FK_TARGET_NON_UNIQUE — Foreign key onto a target no unique key covers
entries.summary: So this is a deploy that breaks today, on the version this package supports, in the configuration a user gets without doing anything.

entries.title: MY.L2.NO_PRIMARY_KEY — InnoDB table left without a primary key
entries.summary: On MySQL a table without a primary key is not a matter of schema taste.

entries.title: MY.L3.ALGORITHM_LOCK_UNEXPRESSIBLE — An operation MySQL will not run online, written the one way that cannot say so
entries.summary: Laravel's MySQL grammar has no way to emit ALGORITHM= or LOCK=.

entries.title: MY.L3.EXCHANGE_PARTITION_CLAUSE_IGNORED — An ALGORITHM or LOCK clause MySQL parses and discards
entries.summary: Every other ALTER TABLE checks the clause and refuses a contradiction. EXCHANGE PARTITION takes it and does nothing.

entries.title: MY.L3.MISSING_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT — A migration that waits for a metadata lock without a bound
entries.summary: MySQL waits a year by default for a metadata lock, and grants those locks in order — so a stuck schema change also stops the reads queued behind it.

entries.title: MY.L3.MIXED_DDL_DML_NOT_ATOMIC — A migration that changes the schema and then writes data
entries.summary: On MySQL, a migration that changes the schema and then writes data is not one operation, whatever you assumed while writing it.

entries.title: MY.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW — A drop breaks whoever is still reading
entries.summary: Dropping a table or column breaks any old application version that still references it.

entries.title: MY.L4.ENUM_CHANGE — Changing an ENUM's member list
entries.summary: MySQL stores an ENUM value as its ordinal position in the member list, not as the string.

entries.title: MY.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT — A column was added and back-filled, and the one it replaces never dropped
entries.summary: Expand is the right first step, and only the first. Until the contract step runs, the table carries two columns for one fact and nothing says which is authoritative.

entries.title: MY.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH — An identifier over MySQL's limit
entries.summary: MySQL refuses the statement with ERROR 1059 and the deploy stops — the rule moves that failure from the deploy to the diff.

entries.title: MY.L5.COLLATION_MIXED — A join across a collation boundary, which costs an index
entries.summary: MySQL converts one side at runtime, and the converted column stops being answerable from its index.

entries.title: MY.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE — A unique key that does not hold, because one of its foreign keys may be NULL
entries.summary: MySQL counts two NULLs as different values, and offers no mode that says otherwise.

entries.title: MY.L5.FLOAT_MONEY — Money in a floating-point column
entries.summary: A float cannot represent 0.10 exactly. The cent goes missing months later, with no way back to the column.

entries.title: MY.L5.SQL_MODE_DIVISION_BY_ZERO_SILENT — a division by zero that answers NULL instead of raising
entries.summary: A MySQL server whose sql_mode omits ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO, so a division by zero that answers NULL instead of raising.

entries.title: MY.L5.SQL_MODE_NOT_STRICT — a truncated value the server called a success
entries.summary: A MySQL server whose sql_mode omits STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, so a truncated value the server called a success.

entries.title: MY.L6.CHARACTER_SET_SERVER_NOT_UTF8MB4 — a default charset that quietly cannot hold your data
entries.summary: Objects created without an explicit CHARACTER SET take the server's, and on latin1 or utf8mb3 they silently alter values MySQL cannot represent.

entries.title: MY.L6.CHARSET_NOT_UTF8MB4 — Text stored under something narrower than utf8mb4
entries.summary: latin1 announces itself; utf8mb3 is the one that looks solved and silently drops every emoji.

entries.title: MY.L6.COLLATION_LEGACY — A utf8mb4 object still sorting by a pre-8.0 collation
entries.summary: utf8mb4_general_ci does not just sort differently — for several languages it sorts wrongly.

entries.title: MY.L6.DEFAULT_STORAGE_ENGINE_NOT_INNODB — a table with no transactions and no foreign keys
entries.summary: A server whose default storage engine is not InnoDB creates tables without transactions, foreign keys or crash recovery when a migration does not name one.

entries.title: MY.L6.EXPLICIT_DEFAULTS_FOR_TIMESTAMP_OFF — legacy TIMESTAMP behavior the migration never asked for
entries.summary: A server with explicit_defaults_for_timestamp off rewrites TIMESTAMP columns on update and turns a written NULL into the current time.

entries.title: MY.L6.INNODB_ROW_FORMAT_NOT_DYNAMIC — the 767-byte ceiling that aborts a deploy halfway
entries.summary: A server creating InnoDB tables as COMPACT gives them a 767-byte index key limit, so the first unique string index fails mid-deploy.

entries.title: MY.L6.LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES_RISK — the development-against-production split you cannot switch off
entries.summary: lower_case_table_names is fixed when a server is initialized, so a mixed-case migration can pass locally and fail in production.

entries.title: MY.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT — An integer primary key too narrow to grow into
entries.summary: The key runs out with no warning, and the fix falls due exactly when it is most expensive.

entries.title: MY.L6.SQL_MODE_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION — a table that quietly got a different storage engine
entries.summary: A MySQL server whose sql_mode omits NO_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION, so a table that quietly got a different storage engine.

entries.title: MY.L6.SQL_MODE_LOOSE_GROUP_BY — a GROUP BY that returns a value from a row nobody chose
entries.summary: A MySQL server whose sql_mode omits ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, so a GROUP BY that returns a value from a row nobody chose.

entries.title: MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_NOT_UTC — a server whose clock is the host's, not a decision
entries.summary: A MySQL server on time_zone = SYSTEM converts timestamps using the host's zone, so the same schema behaves differently on a different machine.

entries.title: MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_TABLES_EMPTY — a named zone the server cannot resolve
entries.summary: A MySQL server on a named time zone whose mysql.time_zone_name holds no rows cannot resolve it, and CONVERT_TZ answers NULL instead of raising.

entries.title: MY.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT — An index whose work another index already does
entries.summary: It answers nothing the wider index cannot, and is still written on every insert.

entries.title: MY.L7.INDEX_UNUSED — An index nobody has read, on an engine that cannot say for how long
entries.summary: performance_schema answers how often; nothing answers since when. That gap decides the rule.

entries.title: MY.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML — A backfill that nothing bounds
entries.summary: A data write in a migration that runs as one statement over however many rows the table happens to hold.

entries.title: MY.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX — A foreign key column Laravel cannot derive a relation from
entries.summary: The convention is what makes a relation resolve with nothing written down; departing from it is legal and costs an explicit key at every call site.

entries.title: MY.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE — An identifier whose meaning depends on the server it lands on
entries.summary: lower_case_table_names differs between a developer machine and a Linux server, so the same migration makes different tables.

entries.title: MY.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT — A table or column with no comment
entries.summary: The most opinionated check in the catalog, and off by default — level 9 is not its gate, a config switch is.

entries.title: MY.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST — A foreign key whose two ends are different types
entries.summary: MySQL refuses the integer case outright, so what survives and still differs is a pair it accepted and converts on every comparison.

entries.title: MY.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR — `SELECT *` in a view definition
entries.summary: A view over a star freezes its column list at creation, so a column added later never appears — and no migration says so.

entries.title: PG.L1.DROP_COLUMN — The old app version is still selecting it
entries.summary: Dropping a column breaks every running release that still reads it, and the data is not coming back.

entries.title: PG.L1.DROP_SCHEMA — Dropping a schema is every table in it at once
entries.summary: DROP SCHEMA is not scoped to one object, and CASCADE reaches past the schema entirely.

entries.title: PG.L1.DROP_TABLE — Dropping a table is a deploy you cannot undo
entries.summary: DROP TABLE takes the rows with it, and CASCADE takes whatever was built on them.

entries.title: PG.L1.TRUNCATE — Emptying a table locks out every reader
entries.summary: TRUNCATE is not a fast DELETE — it takes a lock nobody can read through, and there is no WHERE clause to have forgotten.

entries.title: PG.L2.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED — Adding a constraint scans every row under a lock
entries.summary: ADD CONSTRAINT verifies the whole table before it returns. NOT VALID plus VALIDATE splits that into two cheap halves.

entries.title: PG.L2.DROP_INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT — Dropping an index locks the table, not the index
entries.summary: DROP INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table for the duration. CONCURRENTLY does not.

entries.title: PG.L2.INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT — Building an index blocks every write until it finishes
entries.summary: CREATE INDEX holds a lock against writes for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY does not — and cannot run in a transaction.

entries.title: PG.L2.SET_NOT_NULL_SCAN — Proving no row is null costs a full scan
entries.summary: SET NOT NULL scans the table under its lock. A validated CHECK constraint lets PostgreSQL skip that scan entirely.

entries.title: PG.L2.TYPE_CHANGE_REWRITE — A type change can rewrite the entire table
entries.summary: Unless the new type is binary-coercible from the old one, ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites every row under a lock.

entries.title: PG.L3.CONCURRENTLY_IN_TRANSACTION — CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside Laravel's transaction
entries.summary: PostgreSQL rejects a concurrent index build inside a transaction block, and Laravel opens one for every migration.

entries.title: PG.L3.MISSING_LOCK_TIMEOUT — Without it, the migration waits and everything queues behind it
entries.summary: A lock_timeout aborts your migration instead of stalling the application. That trade is almost always the right one.

entries.title: PG.L3.MISSING_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT — Bounding how long a step may hold what it took
entries.summary: lock_timeout bounds the wait. statement_timeout bounds the hold. A migration needs both.

entries.title: PG.L3.RISKY_OPS_SINGLE_TX — Locks are held until the whole transaction commits
entries.summary: Two locking operations in one migration hold both locks until the last one finishes, not until each one does.

entries.title: PG.L4.CHECK_ENUM_CHANGE — Changing a Laravel enum() column re-checks every row
entries.summary: A Laravel enum() is a varchar with a CHECK. Swapping the constraint validates the whole table under a lock and leaves no rolling-deploy window.

entries.title: PG.L4.CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_PENDING — A constraint was added NOT VALID and never validated
entries.summary: NOT VALID is the right first step, and only the first. Until VALIDATE CONSTRAINT runs, the constraint does not hold for the rows that were already there.

entries.title: PG.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW — The previous release is still running
entries.summary: A drop takes effect on commit. Every instance still serving the old release starts failing at that moment.

entries.title: PG.L4.ENUM_ADD_VALUE — Adding an enum value is a one-way change
entries.summary: PostgreSQL has no ALTER TYPE … DROP VALUE, so down() cannot undo it. A CHECK-constrained column can.

entries.title: PG.L4.ENUM_VALUE_REMOVED — Renaming an enum value rewrites the meaning of stored data
entries.summary: Rows already hold the old name. Renaming the value changes what they mean without touching them.

entries.title: PG.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT — A column was added and back-filled, and the one it replaces never dropped
entries.summary: Expand is the right first step, and only the first. Until the contract step runs, the table carries two columns for one fact and nothing says which is authoritative.

entries.title: PG.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH — An identifier over PostgreSQL's limit
entries.summary: PostgreSQL does not refuse an over-long name, it truncates it and carries on — so the object exists under a name nobody wrote.

entries.title: PG.L4.TYPE_NARROWING — Making a column smaller can lose what is in it
entries.summary: Narrowing asks the server to fit every stored value into a smaller type. It errors, or it truncates.

entries.title: PG.L5.COLLATION_VERSION_MISMATCH — indexes sorted by rules the server no longer uses
entries.summary: A collation whose installed version has moved since the indexes were built can make an equality lookup miss a row that is present.

entries.title: PG.L5.FK_NO_INDEX — Foreign key whose referencing column no index covers
entries.summary: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side of a foreign key and not the referencing one, so every delete on the parent scans the child table.

entries.title: PG.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE — A unique key that does not hold, because one of its foreign keys may be NULL
entries.summary: UNIQUE is one of the few words in SQL people believe without checking. Over a nullable column it constrains nothing.

entries.title: PG.L5.FLOAT_MONEY — Money in a floating-point column
entries.summary: A float cannot represent 0.10 exactly. The cent goes missing months later, with no way back to the column.

entries.title: PG.L5.MONEY_TYPE — The type called money is not the one you want
entries.summary: Its value depends on a server setting, so a restore onto another locale reads the same characters as a different number.

entries.title: PG.L5.NO_PRIMARY_KEY — Table with no primary key and nothing that can stand in for one
entries.summary: A table PostgreSQL cannot identify a row in cannot be replicated, audited, or recovered row by row.

entries.title: PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION_DRIFT — a new error class your code has no reason to handle
entries.summary: Raising the server default changes what every transaction does, including the ones the framework opens for itself.

entries.title: PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_READ_ONLY — the write fails before anything can reason about it
entries.summary: A transaction that does not say READ WRITE refuses writes, and the error reads like a permissions problem without being one.

entries.title: PG.L6.JSON_NOT_JSONB — A json column where jsonb is almost always meant
entries.summary: json re-parses the document on every read and cannot be indexed; jsonb parses once and can. The exception is when the exact bytes matter.

entries.title: PG.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT — An integer primary key too narrow to grow into
entries.summary: The key runs out with no warning, and the fix falls due exactly when it is most expensive.

entries.title: PG.L6.PK_UUID_V4 — Random UUID primary key where PostgreSQL 18 offers a time-ordered one
entries.summary: A v4 UUID primary key scatters inserts across the index; PostgreSQL 18's uuidv7() keeps the uniqueness and adds order.

entries.title: PG.L6.SERIAL_NOT_IDENTITY — A key generated by serial rather than by an identity column
entries.summary: serial is a macro, not a type. Its three pieces can drift apart; an identity column keeps them together.

entries.title: PG.L6.STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS_OFF — the same migration builds two different databases
entries.summary: With it off, a backslash in an ordinary literal escapes the next character. Nothing raises; the row simply holds something else.

entries.title: PG.L6.TIMESTAMP_NO_TZ — Timestamp column with no time zone
entries.summary: A zone-less timestamp stores the digits it was handed and no clock to read them against, and the failure is silent.

entries.title: PG.L6.TIMEZONE_NOT_UTC — a server whose day boundary is somewhere else
entries.summary: The instant is stored correctly either way. What moves is every date cast, every date_trunc and every "today" filter.

entries.title: PG.L7.DATA_CHECKSUMS_DISABLED — corruption from below is returned as data
entries.summary: With checksums on, a damaged page is detected on read. Without them it is handed to your application as a value.

entries.title: PG.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT — An index whose work another index already does
entries.summary: It answers nothing the wider index cannot, and is still written on every insert.

entries.title: PG.L7.INDEX_UNUSED — An index nobody has read, as far as resettable counters can say
entries.summary: The counter is the easy half. The window it covers decides whether the number means anything.

entries.title: PG.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML — A backfill that nothing bounds
entries.summary: A data write in a migration that runs as one statement over however many rows the table happens to hold.

entries.title: PG.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX — A foreign key column Laravel cannot derive a relation from
entries.summary: The convention is what makes a relation resolve with nothing written down; departing from it is legal and costs an explicit key at every call site.

entries.title: PG.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE — An identifier PostgreSQL will not hand back the way you wrote it
entries.summary: An unquoted identifier is folded to lower case, so a mixed-case name means one thing quoted and another unquoted.

entries.title: PG.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT — A table or column with no comment
entries.summary: The most opinionated check in the catalog, and off by default — level 9 is not its gate, a config switch is.

entries.title: PG.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST — A foreign key whose two ends are different types
entries.summary: An int column referencing a bigint key can address only the first 2.1 billion of it — and the day the sequence passes that number is years away.

entries.title: PG.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR — `SELECT *` in a view definition
entries.summary: A view over a star freezes its column list at creation, so a column added later never appears — and no migration says so.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_CLEARTEXT — The password crosses the wire as typed
entries.summary: The `password` auth method sends the credential unhashed and unchallenged.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_MD5 — md5 authentication, whose verifier is the password
entries.summary: The md5 method stores `md5(password || rolname)`, which is crackable offline and usable as-is.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_OPEN_CIDR — The line accepts the whole address space
entries.summary: A host line matching 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 makes every other weakness reachable from anywhere.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_PARSE_ERROR — A line the server could not parse
entries.summary: PostgreSQL rejected a line of pg_hba.conf, so the restriction it was written to impose is not in force.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST — A network line that asks for no password
entries.summary: A `host` line in pg_hba.conf authenticates with `trust`, so anyone who can reach the server is whoever they say they are.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST_LOCAL — Unix-socket connections without authentication
entries.summary: A `local` line authenticates with `trust`, so OS access to the host is database access as any role.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.PASSWORD_LITERAL_IN_MIGRATION — A password written into a migration
entries.summary: The credential is now in version control, in every clone, and in the reflog after somebody removes it in a later commit.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS — An account with no name is an account for anyone
entries.summary: An empty MySQL user name does not mean unused. It matches any name the server does not otherwise know.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS_NO_PASSWORD — No name required, and no password either
entries.summary: The two worst account states at once, and the shortest way into a server that exists.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH — The account's password is stored under a retired verifier
entries.summary: PostgreSQL calls it md5, MySQL calls it mysql_native_password, and MySQL 9.0 removes it outright.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH_LOCKED — A locked account still carrying the retired verifier
entries.summary: Locking an account is not fixing it — unlocking is one statement, and it comes back as it left.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD — The account can log in and has no password at all
entries.summary: A MySQL account on a password plugin with nothing stored under it. Reach the port, know the name, you are in.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD_LOCKED — A locked account with nothing behind the lock
entries.summary: Unlocking is one statement, and what comes back is an account anyone who knows its name can log into.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST — The account may connect from any host
entries.summary: The host half of a MySQL account name is an access control, and `%` matches every address.

entries.title: SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST_PRIVILEGED — Reachable from anywhere, and able to do anything
entries.summary: Either half is ordinary. Together they leave one guessed credential between the network and everything.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG — Every statement is being written down, verbatim
entries.summary: The log does not redact. Passwords and tokens go in as they were sent.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG_PERSONAL_DATA — Row values are being written to the query log
entries.summary: Every WHERE email = … with its value, in a file that outlives the row an erasure request removed.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE — The server may ask the client for a file
entries.summary: The direction is the opposite of what the statement name suggests: the server names the path.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE_FILE_GRANT — The capability and an account that can use it
entries.summary: Two settings that are harmless apart and a route together — reported only when the grant tables could actually be read.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.PASSWORD_ENCRYPTION — New passwords are stored with a deprecated hash
entries.summary: The one md5 finding that reports a server which is clean today — and will not stay that way.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.PATCH_EOL — The server runs a release series that is out of support
entries.summary: Nothing is broken today. The server has simply left the list that receives the fix for whatever is found next.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT — Nothing enforces the encryption the server already offers
entries.summary: Not "encryption is off". A connection that skips it is accepted like any other.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.SECURE_FILE_PRIV — File I/O has no limit, and the value that says so looks like nothing
entries.summary: The empty value is the dangerous one. MySQL writes the switched-off state as the string NULL.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING — Statements and their values are written to the server log
entries.summary: The same setting is good practice on a laptop and a disclosure in production, so this rule asks where it is looking first.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING_SECRETS — Passwords and tokens are going into the server log
entries.summary: CREATE ROLE … LOGIN PASSWORD is logged verbatim. PostgreSQL does not rewrite it.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.TLS_DISABLED — The server does not offer TLS at all
entries.summary: Not "encryption is optional" — no connection to this server can be encrypted, including the one you checked.

entries.title: SEC.CFG.TLS_MIN_VERSION — The server still negotiates a withdrawn TLS version
entries.summary: Everything reports as encrypted. That is what makes this one harder to notice than TLS being off.

entries.title: SEC.INJ.DYNAMIC_IDENTIFIER — A column or sort direction is coming from the request
entries.summary: An identifier is part of the statement, not a value, so it cannot be bound. The only fix is an allowlist — and the rule recognizes the ones you already write.

entries.title: SEC.INJ.RAW_INTERPOLATION — A runtime value was built into the statement instead of bound to it
entries.summary: The property that decides whether an injection is possible at all — reported without ever reading your query.

entries.title: SEC.INJ.RAW_SQL_REASON_STALE — a written reason that no longer covers any raw SQL
entries.summary: The expiry direction. An exemption that outlives its reason reads for years as a decision somebody weighed, and the next reader trusts it.

entries.title: SEC.INJ.RAW_SQL_WITHOUT_REASON — Raw SQL that nobody wrote a reason for
entries.summary: A policy rule, not a vulnerability check. It never reads your query; it asks whether reaching for raw SQL was a decision somebody stated.

entries.title: SEC.PII.UNENCRYPTED_COLUMN — A column that looks like personal data is stored in the clear
entries.summary: The column name matches the privacy dictionary and no Eloquent model casts it to an encrypted type.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.CONNECTIONS_UNSEPARATED — One connection serves requests and deploys migrations
entries.summary: The runtime role holds whatever DDL the migrations need, so an injection inherits it.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ADMIN_IN_MIGRATION — A migration grants an administrative privilege
entries.summary: FILE, PROCESS, RELOAD, SHUTDOWN, CREATE USER and the dynamic SUPER successors govern the server, not the data. An application account needs none of them.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ALL — An account holds every privilege the engine has
entries.summary: There is no privilege escalation left to perform against an account that already has everything.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_EXCESSIVE_IN_MIGRATION — A migration grants everything, or the right to grant it on
entries.summary: Two shapes that are permanent and invisible once they reach the catalog: every privilege on an object, and the option to hand the privilege to somebody else.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_FILE — An account can read and write files as the server
entries.summary: The privilege that turns a SQL injection into a problem on the host, not in the database.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION — The account can hand its access on
entries.summary: WITH GRANT OPTION makes every other limit on the server voluntary.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION_STRUCTURAL — It can hand on the power to change the schema
entries.summary: Not who may read what exists — who may decide what exists.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PROCESS — An account can read every other session's statements
entries.summary: The leak is the statement text, not the session list: anything interpolated rather than bound travels in it.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC — A privilege granted to PUBLIC
entries.summary: PUBLIC is every role that exists and every role that ever will, so a grant to it cannot be reviewed by looking at who has access.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION — A migration grants a privilege to PUBLIC
entries.summary: The catalog rule finds this after it has been applied. This one finds it in the migration, which is the last moment it is still a decision rather than a state.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SCOPE_BROAD_IN_MIGRATION — A grant whose scope is a wildcard
entries.summary: `ON *.*` reaches every database on the server; `ON db.*` reaches every table in one — including the tables added after this migration ran.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SERVER_ADMIN — The account administers the server, not a database
entries.summary: And it does not need SUPER to do it — MySQL 8 split those powers across a family of dynamic privileges.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_WILDCARD_HOST_IN_MIGRATION — A grantee reachable from anywhere
entries.summary: In MySQL the host half of an account is an access control, not a label. `'app'@'%'` is the same credentials with that control removed.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROLE_BYPASSRLS — Row-level security does not apply to this account
entries.summary: The policies are correct and beside the point for an account holding BYPASSRLS.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROLE_CREATEROLE — The account may create roles
entries.summary: It can mint login accounts and administer them — narrower than it used to be, and still a way to keep access.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROLE_SUPERUSER — The account is a superuser, or one SET ROLE away
entries.summary: Superuser is not a strong permission — it is the absence of permission checks.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER — A routine that runs as its owner, correctly
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong here. It is on the report because EXECUTE on this routine is a loan of the owner's rights.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH — EXECUTE means "run code as the owner"
entries.summary: A SECURITY DEFINER routine that does not pin its search_path lets its caller substitute the functions it calls.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGRATION — A definer routine that was never told where to look
entries.summary: The routine runs as its owner while its names resolve against the caller. That is a privilege escalation with no injection and no bug in the function.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH — a pinned search_path is not automatically a safe one
entries.summary: A SECURITY DEFINER routine whose pinned search_path names a schema somebody else can write to, or places pg_temp anywhere but last.

entries.title: SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL — The runtime role may change the schema
entries.summary: An injection that reaches a role with CREATE can leave a table, a function or a trigger behind.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.CHECK_ALWAYS_TRUE — Reads are separated, writes are not
entries.summary: A tenant sees only its own rows and can write a row belonging to anyone.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.DISABLED — A tenant table without row-level security
entries.summary: The table you listed as holding tenant data is readable in full by anything with SELECT.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED — Your policies do not apply to your own connection
entries.summary: The application connects as the role that owns its tables, and owners are exempt.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.NO_POLICY — Row-level security is on and there is no policy
entries.summary: Nothing is exposed; the table is simply unreadable for everyone but its owner.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.OWNER_UNRESTRICTED — The table's owner is exempt from its policies
entries.summary: Your application path is restricted; migrations and console sessions are not.

entries.title: SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE — A policy that lets every row through
entries.summary: Row-level security is on, the table has a policy, and the separation still does not exist.

entries.title: SEC.SKIPPED.* — Part of the security reading was refused
entries.summary: On a managed database this is the ordinary state, and it is stated rather than hidden.

entries.title: SEC.SKIPPED.NOTHING_CHECKED — The security run examined nothing
entries.summary: Not a clean result. A suite that checked nothing has to say so, or its silence reads like a healthy database.
